text: Most people are better at understanding the feelings and sensations that typography and logos give us than they give themselves credit for...even as a non-designer, I think you can look at examples of logos where something's not quite right.
speaker: Jessica Hische
context: Lenny asks Jessica how non-designers can learn to see design through a designer's eyes, since most listeners are product managers, founders, and engineers rather than designers. Jessica explains that people are naturally good at recognizing design patterns and feelings from typography and logos, even if they can't articulate why. She emphasizes that humans constantly absorb visual information as they move through the world, and this gives them an intuitive sense of when something feels "off" about a design, even without formal design training.
text_ko: 대부분 사람들은 자신이 생각하는 것보다 타이포그래피(typography)와 로고(logos)가 주는 느낌과 감각을 더 잘 이해해요. 디자이너가 아니어도 뭔가 좀 이상한 로고 사례를 보면 금방 눈치챌 수 있다고 생각해요.
text_zh: 大多数人比自己想象的更能感受到排版(typography)和标识(logo)传达的那种氛围。就算你不是设计师，只要看几个logo的例子，就能看出哪里不太对劲。
text_es: La mayoría de la gente entiende mejor las sensaciones que nos transmiten la tipografía y los logotipos de lo que creen. Incluso sin ser diseñador, creo que puedes mirar ejemplos de logotipos y ver cuando algo no acaba de encajar.
key_sentence: Most people are better at understanding the feelings and sensations that typography and logos give us than they give themselves credit for.
original_text: Most people are better at understanding the feelings and sensations that typography and logos give us than they give themselves credit for, because what we are as people are endless absorbers of patterns, and information, and all this kind of stuff as we move throughout the world. We don't take time to sit and digest it, but it's still coming in and getting logged, and so even as a non-designer, I think you can look at examples of logos where something's not quite right and be like, "Something's not right here, I just don't know how to name it."

vocabulary.definition: The ability to comprehend or grasp the meaning of something, often involving insight or awareness.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding is crucial for effective communication, decision-making, and fostering relationships among team members and clients.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'understanding' implies a deep comprehension, it can also suggest empathy or emotional intelligence in interpersonal contexts.

vocabulary.definition: Physical feelings or perceptions resulting from stimuli, often related to the senses such as touch, sight, or sound.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and branding, sensations are leveraged to evoke emotional responses from consumers, influencing their purchasing decisions.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often carries a subjective quality, as sensations can vary widely between individuals based on personal experiences.

vocabulary.definition: Specific instances or cases that illustrate a concept, principle, or practice, often used for clarification or demonstration.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business presentations and reports, examples are used to support arguments, showcase best practices, or highlight case studies.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'examples' can provide clarity, they should be relevant and representative to avoid misleading interpretations.

text: I come in then to take the existing vibe and smooth it out, address any of the concerns that came up.
speaker: Jessica Hische
context: Lenny asks Jessica to describe her approach to logo and brand refreshes. Jessica explains her philosophy that startups shouldn't invest heavily in branding from the beginning because they may need to pivot, but once they become successful, they shouldn't be locked into whatever they hastily created for early investor meetings. She describes her role as coming in to refine and professionalize existing branding while maintaining the elements that made it successful in the first place.
text_ko: 그러면 제가 들어가서 기존 분위기(vibe)를 다듬고, 제기된 우려사항들을 짚고 넘어가요.
text_zh: 我进来就是把现有的氛围理顺，把冒出来的顾虑都处理掉。
text_es: Entro para tomar la dinámica que ya hay, suavizarla y atender las preocupaciones que hayan surgido.
key_sentence: take the existing vibe and smooth it out, address any of the concerns that came up.
original_text: I come in then to take the existing vibe and smooth it out, address any of the concerns that came up. A lot of times, it's really utilitarian stuff like this doesn't scale well, or this thing falls apart in this context, or we never had a good avatar version of it, or whatever. Sometimes it's really specific utilitarian fixes, and sometimes it's just about growing it up and sophisticated it without losing what was there in the first place that people got excited about.

vocabulary.definition: To speak to or direct attention to a particular issue or concern.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, 'address' often refers to the act of tackling specific problems or challenges within a project or organization.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'address' implies a proactive approach to resolving issues, it can also suggest that the problem requires careful consideration and discussion.

vocabulary.definition: Issues or worries that require attention or consideration.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business, 'concerns' often refer to stakeholder issues, customer feedback, or internal challenges that need to be managed to ensure smooth operations.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'concerns' carries a sense of urgency and importance, suggesting that these issues could impact decision-making or performance if not addressed.

text: One of the reasons why I tell people why having a custom logo or custom typography can really matter is that if you're using something that's available to everyone, the chances of someone else coming in and copying you are very easy and high.
speaker: Jessica Hische
context: Lenny asks Jessica about signs that it might be time to upgrade from a basic logo to something more professional. Jessica discusses the importance of custom branding, especially when companies are preparing to invest money in physical materials like swag or conference materials. She explains that using widely available fonts or design elements makes it easy for competitors to copy your brand identity, which becomes a bigger risk as companies grow more successful.
text_ko: 제가 맞춤 로고(custom logo)나 맞춤 타이포그래피(custom typography)가 중요하다고 말하는 이유 중 하나는, 누구나 쓸 수 있는 걸 쓰면 누군가가 와서 그대로 따라 하거나 베껴 갈 가능성이 훨씬 높아지기 때문이에요.
text_zh: 我常跟人说，做定制logo（custom logo）或定制字体（custom typography）很重要，原因之一就是如果你用的是人人都能用的东西，别人很容易就来照搬、抄你。
text_es: Una de las razones por las que les digo a mis clientes que tener un logo o una tipografía a medida puede marcar la diferencia es que, si usas algo que cualquiera puede usar, es muy fácil —y bastante probable— que alguien más llegue y te copie.
key_sentence: the chances of someone else coming in and copying you are very easy and high.
original_text: One of the reasons why I tell people why having a custom logo or custom typography can really matter is that if you're using something that's available to everyone, the chances of someone else coming in and copying you are very easy and high. You might be one of these lucky companies that just out the gate is outrageously successful, but with success comes people climbing up behind you trying to copy your success.

vocabulary.definition: Available to everyone means that a product, service, or resource is accessible to all individuals without restrictions or limitations.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, offerings that are available to everyone can enhance market reach and inclusivity, but may also lead to increased competition and dilution of brand uniqueness.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often carries a connotation of commonality, suggesting that widespread availability may undermine exclusivity or perceived value.

text: I'm not opposed to Frankensteining options together.
speaker: Jessica Hische
context: Lenny mentions that during their logo refresh process, he changed direction after they had narrowed down options, asking to go back and explore different approaches. Jessica explains her flexible approach to client feedback, using a cooking metaphor to describe how she designs logo elements that can be combined in different ways. She contrasts her method with other designers who might be more rigid about not mixing different design directions together.
text_ko: 옵션들을 프랑켄슈타인식(Frankensteining)으로 짜맞춰 쓰는 데 반대하지 않아요.
text_zh: 我不反对把不同选项拼凑在一起试试。
text_es: No me cierro a combinar opciones a lo Frankenstein (Frankensteining).
key_sentence: I'm not opposed to Frankensteining options together.
original_text: I'm not opposed to Frankensteining options together. To me, it's like I'm giving you a menu of all the things that we can do, but I'm like a chef that puts a menu together where you can combine different appetizers and different mains and they all still make sense. Some people will give you a menu and if you try to do that, it's insane and it tastes terrible. But for me, everything that we're doing, I feel like, mixes and matches fairly well.

vocabulary.definition: Choices or alternatives available in a particular situation or context.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, options often refer to different strategies, products, or solutions that a company can pursue to meet objectives or respond to market conditions.
vocabulary.nuance: The term carries a connotation of flexibility and choice, suggesting that having multiple options can lead to better decision-making and innovation.

text: I feel like a lot of clients come to me and they have hot ham water when it comes to their brand. It's just about turning that into a soup, something that feels real.
speaker: Jessica Hische
context: Jessica uses a cooking analogy to explain brand cohesion, comparing her move from New York (where she never cooked) to San Francisco (where she learned to cook). She describes how early cooking attempts result in ingredients that don't work together, but with experience you learn to create cohesive dishes. She applies this to branding, explaining that many clients come to her with disparate brand elements that don't feel unified, and her job is to make everything feel like it was created together.
text_ko: 많은 클라이언트들이 제게 오면 자기 브랜드에 대해 사실상 실체가 없는, '핫 햄 워터(hot ham water)' 같은 상태를 가지고 오는 것 같아요. 제 일은 그걸 수프처럼 실감 나고 진짜로 느껴지는 무언가로 바꿔주는 거예요.
text_zh: 我发现很多客户来找我的时候，他们的品牌就像是泡火腿的水一样，没什么味道。我要做的就是把它变成一锅好汤，让人感觉有血有肉的。
text_es: Siento que muchos clientes llegan a mí con una marca que está como agua tibia con jamón, ¿sabes? Se trata de convertir eso en una sopa de verdad, algo que se sienta auténtico.
key_sentence: Clients often have hot ham water; I help turn it into something real.

vocabulary.definition: A subjective perception that something is authentic, genuine, or believable.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and branding, creating experiences or products that 'feel real' can enhance customer engagement and loyalty by fostering emotional connections.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase conveys a sense of authenticity and relatability, making it particularly effective in discussions about customer experience or product design.

text: It's cool because you are reverse-justifying decisions. I think that's a really fun exercise to do, is to Song Exploder your intuition.
speaker: Jessica Hische
context: Jessica continues explaining how people can develop their design intuition by examining why certain fonts or designs make them feel specific ways. She suggests that feelings about design often come from personal associations - for example, a font might remind someone of being 22 at a band show, which creates a specific emotional response. She encourages people to analyze their intuitive reactions to understand the underlying reasons for their design preferences.
text_zh: 挺酷的，因为你是在事后为决策找理由。我觉得把直觉像《Song Exploder》(Song Exploder)那样拆解来分析，挺好玩的练习。
text_es: Me parece genial porque justificas las decisiones al revés. Creo que es un ejercicio realmente divertido: desmenuzar tu intuición al estilo "Song Exploder" (Song Exploder).
key_sentence: Reverse-justifying decisions is a fun exercise to Song Exploder your intuition.
original_text: It's cool because you are reverse-justifying decisions. I think that's a really fun exercise to do, is to Song Exploder your intuition. You make a decision intuitively or look at something and intuit what you feel from it, and then really try to dive in, "Why do I feel that way? What could this have reminded me of that made me feel that way?"

vocabulary.definition: The ability to understand something instinctively, without the need for conscious reasoning.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup ecosystem, intuition often guides entrepreneurs in decision-making, especially in uncertain or rapidly changing environments.
vocabulary.nuance: Intuition can be seen as a valuable asset, but relying solely on it may undermine data-driven decision-making.

vocabulary.definition: An activity or task designed to develop a skill or improve performance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate setting, exercises are often used in training sessions to enhance team collaboration, problem-solving, and critical thinking skills.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'exercise' can imply a structured approach to learning, but it may also suggest a lack of seriousness if not framed appropriately.

text: My goal always when designing a logo is to design a logo that's so easy to use that you don't have to be an extremely skilled designer to design well with it.
speaker: Jessica Hische
context: Jessica explains her philosophy about creating user-friendly brand assets. She discusses how some companies need extensive brand guidelines because their logos are complex, but her approach is different - she aims to create logos that are intuitive to use correctly. She believes that since most startups don't have dedicated brand teams or expert designers, the logo itself should guide people toward using it properly without requiring extensive training or documentation.
text_ko: 제가 로고(logo)를 디자인할 때 항상 목표는 사용하기 너무 쉬워서 굉장히 숙련된 디자이너가 아니어도 잘 활용해 좋은 결과를 낼 수 있게 만드는 거예요.
text_zh: 我做标志（logo）设计时的目标一直很简单：把它做得足够好用，让不是特别资深的设计师也能用它做出好设计。
text_es: Mi objetivo al diseñar un logotipo es que sea tan fácil de usar que no haga falta ser un diseñador muy habilidoso para lograr buenos resultados con él.
key_sentence: My goal is to design logos easy to use, even without a rock star designer.
original_text: My goal always when designing a logo is to design a logo that's so easy to use that you don't have to be an extremely skilled designer to design well with it. That's my number one goal, because I know not everybody is going to be at a stage where they have an internal brand team or a designer that's a rock star designer that can work with really complicated assets and make them look good.
